maths_errors.text: The measured value itself does not determine the bounds — the rounding unit does.
maths_errors.correction: Taken literally this is false. The bounds are 94 − 0.5 and 94 + 0.5, so they depend on the measured value. What the rounding unit alone decides is the amount added and subtracted (half the precision). Reword to: "The amount you add and subtract comes from the rounding unit, not from the measured value."

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Basic foundation: round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy (eg to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures)
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never teaches how to round a number to a given number of decimal places or significant figures. It assumes the student can already do this and only works backwards from a rounded value.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Additional foundation: use inequality notation to specify simple error intervals due to truncation or rounding
missing_spec_content.why: Truncation is not mentioned anywhere. The formula 'measured value ± ½ × precision' does not work for truncation: 8.3 truncated to 1 d.p. gives 8.3 ≤ x < 8.4. The student is given no method for this case.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Notes: including appropriate rounding for questions set in context. Students should know not to round values during intermediate steps of a calculation.
missing_spec_content.why: Neither rounding sensibly in context (for example, giving an answer to a suitable accuracy) nor keeping full accuracy during intermediate steps is taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Higher only: including upper and lower bounds
missing_spec_content.why: At Higher tier this means using bounds in calculations: the greatest or least value of a sum, difference, product or quotient, and choosing a suitable degree of accuracy by comparing upper and lower bounds. slides[1].whenToUse mentions 'the greatest/least possible value of a calculation', but the lesson never teaches how to do it.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Additional foundation: apply and interpret limits of accuracy
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only finds bounds for a single value. It never applies or interprets limits of accuracy in a problem, for example checking whether items will fit or stating what a result tells you.

cases_not_modelled.why: No example shows truncation, which needs a different interval from rounding.

cases_not_modelled.case: Rounding to significant figures (e.g. 3400 to 2 s.f.)
cases_not_modelled.why: No worked example works out the precision from significant figures, where the unit may be 100, 0.01 and so on.

cases_not_modelled.case: Rounding to decimal places in a worked example
cases_not_modelled.why: The only decimal case (3.7 cm to 1 d.p.) appears as a common mistake. It is never worked step by step.

cases_not_modelled.case: Rounding to the nearest 10, 100 or other non-unit precision (e.g. nearest 5)
cases_not_modelled.why: The only worked example uses a precision of 1.

cases_not_modelled.case: Rounding a number to a given accuracy (forward direction)
cases_not_modelled.why: No example rounds a number. Every example starts from a value that is already rounded.

cases_not_modelled.case: Bounds of a sum or difference (e.g. upper bound of a − b uses UB of a and LB of b)
cases_not_modelled.why: Not modelled, although the formula slide promises it.

cases_not_modelled.case: Bounds of a product or quotient (e.g. upper bound of a ÷ b uses UB of a and LB of b)
cases_not_modelled.why: Not modelled. This is a standard Higher question.

cases_not_modelled.case: Choosing a suitable degree of accuracy from upper and lower bounds
cases_not_modelled.why: Not modelled. This is a standard Higher question.

cases_not_modelled.case: Interpreting limits of accuracy in context
cases_not_modelled.why: Not modelled. There is no example that uses bounds to make a decision or reach a conclusion.

density.text: Bounds define that range: the lower bound is the smallest value that rounds to the given measurement, and the upper bound is the smallest value that would round up to the next value.
density.why: One sentence defines 'bounds', the lower bound and the upper bound. The upper-bound definition is also hard to follow: the upper bound is described as a value that does not round to the measurement, and the sentence never says that it is excluded from the interval.

density.text: The error interval is written as: lower bound ≤ value < upper bound — note the strict inequality at the upper end, because the upper bound itself would round up.
density.why: One sentence gives the notation, introduces the term 'strict inequality' without explaining it, and gives the reason for using it.

density.text: 93.5 ≤ l < 94.5 — the lower bound uses ≤ (the lower bound itself rounds to 94), the upper bound uses < (94.5 would round up to 95).
density.why: One line holds the answer and two separate reasons in brackets. The variable l appears here for the first time without being defined.

density.text: Identify the precision (the rounding unit) first — it determines the ±0.5 unit adjustment.
density.why: '±0.5 unit adjustment' can be read as 'always add and subtract 0.5'. That is exactly the mistake warned against in slides[3].mistakes[2] (±0.05 for 1 d.p.). It should say 'half of the rounding unit'.
